parts:
You're right, and the reason is sharper than "some arguments use symmetry": the appendix is answering a different question than the one your program asks. It asks *which extension is canonical* (uniqueness/normalization). You need *existence of a member of a rigid class*. Those come apart, and the appendix's symmetry hypotheses are exactly what makes them look connected.

## The audit

- **Theorem A (multiplicative rigidity)** — genuinely symmetry-free. No equivariance, no regularity, only pointwise multiplicativity + normalization + continuity in $f$. It concludes equivariance rather than assuming it. This one binds you: any class arising as the image of a product-preserving extension *operator* is slice regular, full stop. But it constrains operators, not functions or classes — and you only need one function.
- **§4 (axial Vekua) and §5 (linear classification)** — equivariance is load-bearing everywhere, plus linearity in $f$ and Fueter regularity as the target. Three assumptions you want to drop. Nothing here reaches your setting.
- **§6 (twistor)** — the operative hypothesis is *fibration-compatibility*, which forces the product form $F\times\mathrm{id}$ and hence all the rigidity. That's a choice, not a necessity. The antipodal condition $G\circ a = a\circ G$ is not the symmetry you object to; it's forced by descent to $\mathbb{H}$ and you can't drop it. But holomorphic *bundles* or *divisors* on $Q$ (or on $\mathbb{CP}^3$) that aren't of product type are entirely untouched — which is where the YM detour was actually pointing.

So: one of four sections survives your objection, and it constrains something you weren't proposing.

## The one result that *is* aimed at your shape — and it's negative

Corollary A.11 (Vekua mismatch) says: equivariant + Fueter regular + holomorphic on a slice $\Rightarrow$ constant. That isn't a uniqueness statement, it's a **nonexistence** statement, and it's exactly the shape you need to worry about. The mechanism is worth extracting because it's portable: equivariance forces the axial form $A(x,r) + \omega B(x,r)$, and then *any* first-order linear system picks up the transverse-trace term $-\tfrac{2}{r}B$ — the $2$ being the transverse dimension count. Holomorphic slice data satisfies the *uncorrected* Cauchy–Riemann system. The two differ by exactly that term, so they're incompatible.

That gives you a cheap test to run on any candidate class before investing in it: write the equivariant reduction, see whether the trace term can be absorbed. For linear PDE-defined classes, rigidity up means existence down, mechanically.

## The problem that has nothing to do with the appendix

This is the one I'd want you to sit with. For *any* equivariant $F$, the off-axis zero set is $\{A = B = 0\} \times S^2$ — a union of spheres, automatically, by the axial form. So for the symmetric member of your class, "zeros are isolated" is not a consequence you derive from membership; it is verbatim the statement that $\Xi$ has no non-real zeros. The class contributes the step "symmetric + isolated $\Rightarrow$ real", which is a triviality. All the load is on the existence theorem.

And that theorem must fail for $z^2+1$ — if $f$ has a non-real zero, equivariance propagates it to a sphere, contradicting the class. So any hypothesis $P$ in "$f$ has $P$ $\Rightarrow$ $f$ admits a symmetric $\mathcal{C}$-extension" satisfies $P \Rightarrow$ hyperbolicity. You get a criterion factory, not a mechanism — unless $P$ is something independently provable for $\Xi$, which is the same wall as memo 6 §3 wearing analytic clothes instead of arithmetic ones.

That said: Weil positivity is also "just" a criterion, and in char $p$ the criterion got proved. So this locates the difficulty rather than closing the route.

## A real gap in the appendix, and it's the shape you asked for

Remark A.7 claims uniqueness from slice data "can only come from symmetry or from holomorphic geometry upstairs — never from ellipticity alone." As stated that's false, and the counterexample is close to what you want. The argument implicitly treats the slice as a *complex* line, which it is for slice regularity. Choose differently: fix $\eta \perp I_0$ and give $\mathbb{H}$ the complex structure $J_\eta(q) = q\eta$. Then $\mathbb{C}_{I_0} = \mathrm{span}\{1, I_0\}$ is a **maximal totally real** 2-plane in $(\mathbb{H}, J_\eta) \cong \mathbb{C}^2$. Restriction from $J_\eta$-holomorphic maps to the slice is then a bijection — unique extension by complexification, and entire data gives entire extensions. The codimension-2 polarity objection evaporates because $\bar\partial F = 0$ for a map $\mathbb{C}^2 \to \mathbb{C}^2$ is *overdetermined*, not determined.

And this class forbids zero spheres for free: $\mathbb{C}^2$ is Stein, so no compact analytic subset, so no $S^2$ inside a zero curve. Concretely, for intrinsic data with stem $G$, in coordinates $\zeta_\pm = z_1 \pm iw$ the extension is $A = \tfrac12(G(\zeta_+)+G(\zeta_-))$, $B = \tfrac{1}{2i}(G(\zeta_+)-G(\zeta_-))$, so

$$Z(F) = Z(G) \times Z(G),$$

always discrete. (I checked $f = q^2$ by hand: $F = (z_1^2 - w^2,\, 2z_1w)$, zero set the single point.) So a rigid, non-equivariant, isolated-zeros class with existence *and* uniqueness does exist.

The catch is where you'd expect: $J_\eta$ breaks $SO(3)$ to the $U(1)$ fixing $\eta$, whose orbits are circles, not spheres — and circles sit inside complex curves without obstruction. What you get instead is that an off-axis zero forces $Z(F)$ to be positive-dimensional, i.e. $A$ and $B$ to share a factor. And the reality of $\rho \in Z(G)$ turns out to be exactly $\tau$-fixedness of the diagonal point $(\rho,\rho)$ under $\tau(\zeta_+,\zeta_-) = (\bar\zeta_-,\bar\zeta_+)$ — which is the crunode/acnode invariant of the twistor note §3 again, in a much simpler setting. Rigidity is genuinely free here; the discriminant relocates rather than resolves.

## Where I'd actually look

**Demand symmetry of the zero set, not of the function.** You never needed $F(uq\bar u) = uF(q)\bar u$; you needed $Z(F)$ rotation-invariant. That's far weaker — twisted equivariance $F(uq\bar u) = g\,F(q)\,h$ with $g,h$ nonvanishing, or $F$ a section of a bundle, or projective equivariance — and it dodges the axial-form collapse entirely, because $F$ need not have the form $A + \omega B$. Every symmetry-based argument in the appendix assumes the strong version. Note your own twistor note already found the discriminating invariant in exactly this language ($\sigma$-type of divisor components, $\mathbb{RP}^2$ vs $S^2$ in $Y$) — that's a zero-set condition, not a function condition.

**Nonlinearity.** The trace-term obstruction is a linear phenomenon. Symmetric reductions of nonlinear equations carry $1/r$ terms as a matter of course and have nontrivial solutions — Bogomolny/monopole being the obvious case. That's the one place the existence half can survive real rigidity, and it's a defensible reason the Yang–Mills excursion wasn't a wrong turn.

The honest bottom line: the appendix does not rule out your original line, but it also isn't what's standing in the way. What's standing in the way is that the symmetric member's existence carries the entire proof, and that's an analytic statement about $\Xi$, not a geometric one. The loophole worth probing is zero-divisor symmetry in a rigid non-equivariant class — the totally-real-complexification computation above is the smallest concrete instance, and it's cheap to push further.

Want me to verify that computation symbolically and write it up as a short memo 7? It's a genuine correction to Remark A.7 either way, independent of whether the route revives.

parts:
Yes — with one correction to the mechanism, and the corrected version is stronger than what you said.

## Why your instinct is structurally right

The failure mode you kept hitting is specific to *linear* overdetermination. For a linear system, "rigid" means the solution space is a small vector space, and small vector spaces of functions are spanned by low-degree polynomials. Rigidity and triviality are the same thing there — you can't tune your way out of it.

For a nonlinear self-duality equation the solution set isn't a vector space at all. "Rigid" means finite-dimensional *moduli* with discrete invariants, and the elements can be as complicated as you like. Charge-$k$ $SU(2)$ instantons on $\mathbb{R}^4$ form an $(8k-3)$-dimensional moduli space — small, but nothing in it is trivial. So nonlinearity buys you exactly the thing you couldn't get: constraint without collapse.

The abelian case makes this sharp in the direction you're pointing. $U(1)$ anti-self-duality on $\mathbb{R}^4$ *is* linear — it's just ASD Maxwell — and it has no finite-energy instantons at all ($H^2(S^4) = 0$, so the field is flat). The nonabelian nonlinearity isn't decoration on top of a linear theory; it's the entire reason the moduli space is nonempty. That's a cleaner statement of your point than the 2D one.

## The correction

"In 2D the nonlinearities become scalars and get absorbed into linear equations" is right for a subfamily and misleading in general. Liouville's equation (the $SU(2)$ Hitchin reduction) genuinely linearizes via holomorphic data. But KdV, NLS, sine-Gordon — all reductions of ASDYM by Ward's correspondence — are not linearizable. What's true of all of them is something better for your purposes: **the nonlinear equation is equivalent to linear data in an auxiliary space.** Downstairs that's a Lax pair / inverse scattering. Upstairs it's Ward's theorem: ASD connections on a domain in $\mathbb{R}^4$ correspond to holomorphic vector bundles on the corresponding region of twistor space, trivial on the real lines.

So the right picture isn't "nonlinear generalizes linear." It's: one-variable complex analysis is the **rank-one** case of holomorphic bundle geometry on twistor space, and the nonlinear field equations downstairs are what rank $\geq 2$ looks like when you push it back down. You're not leaving the holomorphic category by going nonlinear — you're widening it from functions to bundles.

And that's exactly the loophole from last time. Dropping fibration-compatibility meant "holomorphic objects on $Q$ that aren't product-form self-maps," and bundles are the natural such objects. Your instinct and that gap are the same gap.

## Why ADHM is actually apt, not just nostalgia

Here's the part that made me sit up. The reality condition in the ADHM/Atiyah–Ward setup is: the bundle on twistor space is trivial on every *real* line — equivalently, **no jumping lines over real points.** Barth's theorem says the jumping lines of a charge-$k$ instanton bundle form a degree-$k$ divisor in the Klein quadric, and the real structure $\sigma$ acts on it.

Compare your twistor note §3: the discriminating invariant is the $\sigma$-action on the components of a divisor in the space of lines — $\sigma$-fixed components (real zeros, $\mathbb{RP}^2$ downstairs) versus $\sigma$-swapped pairs (zero spheres, $S^2$). Same invariant, same space, opposite polarity. The instanton condition is "no $\sigma$-fixed components in the jumping divisor"; RH is "all components $\sigma$-fixed."

That's the first time in this program that the structure you want has appeared somewhere it's *already governed by a positivity condition on finite quaternionic matrix data* — which is what ADHM is. And it addresses memo 6 §4 head on: the decisive objection there was that the reality involution on a zero multiset gives you a **commutative** algebra with trivial involution, making the positivity circular. ADHM data is not commutative. $[B_1,B_2] + ij = 0$ and $[B_1,B_1^*] + [B_2,B_2^*] + ii^* - j^*j = 0$ are noncommutative moment-map equations with a genuine positivity flavor. Hitchin's spectral-curve conditions for monopoles have the same shape — reality $\sigma(S)=S$ plus a vanishing condition $H^0 = 0$ that plays the role of nondegeneracy.

So: memo 6's *decisive* finding is the one thing on this route that might actually be circumventable.

## What it doesn't fix, stated plainly

Three things survive intact, and two of them are the ones that closed the program:

1. **Rationality (memo 6 §3, §6).** Any ADHM data built from $\Xi$ has entries that are moments of $\Phi$. Noncommutativity is now available; $\mathbb{Q}$-structure still isn't, and no amount of gauge theory manufactures it. This is untouched.
2. **Softness.** Charge $k$ and the degree of the jumping divisor are deformation invariants — precisely the class your §4 no-go already killed (homology class *and* quaternionic winding both weight spheres by 2; Davenport–Heilbronn passes any deformation-invariant test). If the route lands on charge, it's dead on arrival. It has to land on the $\sigma$-type of components, which is not deformation-invariant.
3. **Finite charge versus infinitely many zeros.** $\Xi$ has infinitely many zeros; ADHM data has finite charge. You'd need either a limit (calorons, infinite-rank monads) or truncations — and limits are where this kind of thing usually dies.

## The cheap test I'd run first

Point 3 has an obvious dictionary candidate that makes the whole thing a finite computation: Jensen/Hadamard truncations $\Xi_N$ are real polynomials of degree $2N$, your note §5c already puts them in the Klein quadric as degree-$2N$ curves, and charge-$k$ instantons carry degree-$k$ jumping divisors. So:

> Attach ADHM-type data to the Jensen truncation $J^{d,n}$ for $d = 2, 3$. Two questions, both decidable by hand or with sympy. **(a)** Does the algebra generated by the data actually fail to commute? **(b)** Is the positivity condition that corresponds to "all jumping-divisor components $\sigma$-fixed" derivable from the moment-map equations, or is it Sylvester's law again in disguise?

If (a) comes out commutative, memo 6 §4 applies verbatim and this closes in an afternoon — which is worth knowing, because it's the strongest remaining hope. If (a) is noncommutative and (b) is non-circular, you have the first thing in eleven years that has the shape of Weil's argument rather than a relabeling of it, and the remaining gap is rationality — a known, named, hard problem rather than a hidden tautology.

That's a good use of a session, and the downside is bounded. Want me to set it up? I'd write it as `lab_adhm_check.py` plus a memo, in the same style as the tower check, and I'd rather compute (a) before writing a word of prose about (b).

Done — and it split cleanly, which is the good outcome.

**(a) Yes.** The ADHM variety is genuinely noncommutative. Reality of $\Delta^\dagger\Delta$ turns out to force exactly the classical ADHM package — all four real blocks of $T$ symmetric, plus $[T_0,T_a] - \epsilon_{abc}[T_b,T_c] + \mathrm{Im}_a(\lambda^\dagger\lambda) = 0$ — and that variety has solutions with nonvanishing commutators everywhere (120/120 exact solutions at $k=2,3,4$, plus an exact rational witness: $T_0 = \begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}$, $T_1 = \mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$, $\lambda = (1, 2i)$). The positivity comes free: $C = \sum_a T_a^2 + \mathrm{Re}(\lambda^\dagger\lambda) \succeq 0$ is a sum of squares plus a Gram matrix. So memo 6 §4's objection genuinely is not automatic here — ADHM was the right thing to look at.

**(b) No, and provably.** Requiring the real jumping locus to be the zero set of a slice extension — $\det(\Delta^\dagger\Delta) = p(x_0+ir)p(x_0-ir)$ — forces $\lambda = 0$ and $T_1 = T_2 = T_3 = 0$. The data collapses onto the commutative real locus, and then "$p$ hyperbolic" is the spectral theorem for one real symmetric matrix.

The proof is short: restrict to a slice, continue $y \to i\eta$, substitute $u = x_0+\eta$, $v = x_0-\eta$, and the identity becomes $\det(uvI - uN - v\bar N + C) = p(u)p(v)$ with $N = T_0 + iT_e$. The $u^k$ coefficient gives $p = \det(vI - N)$ for every unit imaginary $e$; the $u^{k-1}v^{k-1}$ coefficient gives $\mathrm{tr}\,C = \mathrm{tr}\,T_0^2 + \mathrm{tr}\,T_e^2$ for every $e$. Independence of $e$ forces $\mathrm{tr}(T_aT_b) = \kappa\delta_{ab}$, and comparing with $\mathrm{tr}\,C = \mathrm{tr}\,T_0^2 + 3\kappa + \|\lambda\|^2$ gives $2\kappa + \|\lambda\|^2 = 0$. Both terms are non-negative.

Two things worth flagging. First, an adversarial review pass reproduced it and found it's **stronger** than I first wrote: the nonlinear ADHM equations are never used, nor is $C \succeq 0$ — only the linear part of the reality condition. The collapse happens before the interesting structure is consulted. There's also an exact ideal-membership certificate at $k=2$ for symbolic monic $p$: modulo the affine-linear coefficient equations, $2\sum \mathrm{tr}\,T_a^2 + 3\|\lambda\|^2$ is a rational combination of four of the rest.

Second, the numerics agree independently — 12/12 cases, existence tracking hyperbolicity, including a correct NO for your memo-5 quartic (whose conjugate pair sits at $\pm 0.0088$ and which *passes* the Newton/Turán test). The residual floor there is $10^{-3}$ against $10^{-13}$ for hyperbolic targets, degrading continuously with sphere radius, matching the $j_\ell(\lambda y_0)$ behaviour you predicted in the twistor note.

One incidental finding I'd single out, because it's the third independent time the same thing has shown up: my first version of the last test used off-axis points that all happened to lie in a single slice, and there $\det M$ and $P_p$ agreed exactly — the datum was just the $x_0 \leftrightarrow x_1$ rotation of the hyperbolic solution. One slice cannot tell which axis is the real one. The discriminating power isn't "off the real axis," it's off any single slice, carried by the full 2-sphere of complex structures. Same conclusion the appendix reached from uniqueness and the twistor note reached from the divisor.

I've written this up as `memo7_adhm_test.md` in the project, updated item 5 of `PROGRAM_CLOSED.md`, and saved the lab code. One caution recorded there: given the novelty lesson from the oscillation lemma, I'd assume the §4 theorem is known until swept — it's a rigidity statement about symmetric determinantal representations, and that's Lax-conjecture/Helton–Vinnikov territory. It's an internal certification of a no-go, not a result.

parts:
Worth doing — the relaxation fails, but it produced the best single result of this whole arc, because the failure is now an exact formula rather than a plateau.

**One-slice matching is completely characterised, and completely contentless.** Requiring $\det(\Delta^\dagger\Delta) = P_p$ on a single slice $\Pi_e$ forces $\lambda = 0$, $T_a = e_a S$ for one real symmetric $S$, and $[T_0,S] = 0$ — the data becomes commutative and $\mathbb{C}_e$-valued — and then $p = \det(zI - (T_0+iS))$, which realises **every** real monic $p$, hyperbolic or not. So it's worse than the full matching on both counts at once: no discriminating power, and the noncommutativity still dies. Verified exactly for $z^2+1$, $z^2+z+1$, $(z-1)((z+2)^2+9)$, repeated roots, and your memo-5 quartic.

**But here's the payoff.** Inside that family there's an exact formula. Diagonalise $(T_0,S)$ jointly with eigenvalues $\tau_j, \sigma_j$, set $t = \langle\operatorname{Im}q, e\rangle$, $r = |\operatorname{Im}q|$, $B_j = (x_0-\tau_j)^2 + r^2 + \sigma_j^2$:

$$\det M(q) = \prod_j(B_j - 2t\sigma_j), \qquad P_p(q) = \prod_j(B_j - 2r\sigma_j).$$

The two differ **only** in $t$ versus $r$. Conjugate pairing makes every factor strictly decreasing, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives $t^2 \le r^2$ with equality *exactly on the slice*. So $\det M - P_p > 0$ everywhere off $\Pi_e$ whenever $S \ne 0$, and vanishes identically when $S = 0$.

Three things fall out. The threshold isn't two slices — **one slice plus a single off-slice point** already forces hyperbolicity ($p = z^2+1$: residual $0.42$ with one extra point, versus $10^{-15}$ without). The forcing is non-uniform, degrading as $O(\theta^2)$ in the angle between slices — so any *approximate* two-slice condition with tolerance $\varepsilon$ lets non-hyperbolic $p$ through once $\varepsilon \gtrsim \theta^2$, which is the same softness as the $j_\ell(\lambda y_0)$ decay in your twistor note. And the whole discriminant is $r^2 - t^2$, weighted by the imaginary parts of the roots.

That last point is the transferable one, and it's a cheap test for anything future: **if a condition can be stated slice by slice, it carries no information about reality of zeros.** The information lives on the 2-sphere directions transverse to every slice, and a slice is precisely where the discriminant vanishes — blind by construction, not merely weak.

Two smaller findings. I also tested the other natural reading — drop matching entirely and use the quaternionic right-eigenvalue classes of $T$, which are 2-spheres unless real, so the zero-sphere structure is native. ADHM reality makes $T$ quaternionic *symmetric*, not *Hermitian*, so the spectral theorem doesn't apply, and empirically every admissible datum at $k=2,3,4$ has non-real classes (median $|\mathrm{Im}|/\|T\| \approx 1.4$–$1.8$). Spheres allowed, so no isolation, so nothing to contradict. And within the relaxed family, "$p$ hyperbolic" is exactly "$T_0 + iS$ self-adjoint" — the relaxation lands on the Hilbert–Pólya statement, with the geometry contributing nothing on top of a reformulation that was already available without it. Notable since that's the one route `PROGRAM_CLOSED.md` records as *not* closed.

Two corrections from the adversarial pass, both recorded: my first characterisation was missing a sufficiency condition (the joint spectrum must be $\sigma \mapsto -\sigma$ invariant, else $p$ isn't real — $T_0=0$, $S=\mathrm{diag}(1,2)$ is the counterexample), and I had the threshold at two slices when it's really one point. Also worth flagging: $\lambda = 0$ in both memo 7 and memo 8 means the last row of $\Delta$ vanishes, so the matched data isn't a *regular* ADHM datum at all — it sits outside the instanton moduli space, not just on its commutative locus.

Filed as `memo8_slice_relaxation.md` with the code and log, and I added the cheap test to `PROGRAM_CLOSED.md` so a future session doesn't re-propose the relaxation. Same novelty caveat as before — this is elementary stuff about commuting real symmetric pairs and Cauchy–Schwarz, and the deficit formula smells like something that falls out of standard axial-monogenic computations. Assume known.

One reflection: this is the fourth independent time "the information is in the transverse sphere directions" has come up — the appendix's $-2B/r$ trace term, the twistor note's $\sigma$-type of divisor components, memo 7's rotated-frame degeneracy, and now the exact $r^2 - t^2$. Your original design already knew this, in the sense that it *needed* rotational symmetry to turn one off-axis zero into a sphere. What's new is that the trade-off is now exact: constraint and collapse are driven by the same quantity, so there's no sweet spot between them.

parts:
Yes, it makes sense — with one caveat.

**The caveat.** Three slice-regular results are load-bearing for the *new* direction, not because they're about slice regularity but because they're the no-gos that tell you what not to try: multiplicative rigidity (kills any functional-calculus construction, and it assumes no symmetry and no regularity), the linear no-go (any discriminating functional must be nonlinear), and the Vekua trace term (the cleanest instance of the central principle). I've carried those forward as a short "inherited constraints" section rather than dropping them. Everything else slice-regular is gone.

**Structure of the brief.** §1 states the strategy precisely and proves the no-free-lunch proposition — any route of this shape is a hyperbolicity criterion factory, so the whole weight sits on existence, and that dictates where to aim. §2 is the real asset: the transverse-sphere principle with four independent derivations and the exact $r^2 - t^2$ formula. §3 is the rigidity/existence trade-off. §4 is the ADHM work with full proofs and conventions. §5 is new (below). §6 is the inherited constraints including the rationality wall. §7 is live directions, §8 is a nine-step screening checklist, §9 is reference data and the code inventory.

**What the verification turned up.** I finally checked the totally-real complexification I'd sketched in my first reply, and it does refute the appendix's Remark A.7 — a slice is a *complex line* for $J_{I_0}$ but *maximally totally real* for $J_\eta$ with $\eta \perp I_0$, so restriction is a bijection, uniqueness comes from overdetermined ellipticity, and $Z(F) = Z(G) \times Z(G)$ is always discrete. Isolation is free, no symmetry assumed. That's exactly the class shape you wanted.

But it fails, and the failure is the thing worth having. The class is preserved only by the circle fixing $\eta$, whose fixed locus in $\mathbb{H}$ is a slice. A discrete set invariant under a connected group must lie in the fixed locus. And $Z(G) \times Z(G)$ has off-diagonal points outside it — so even invariance of the zero *set*, the weakest hypothesis that still manufactures spheres, is **unsatisfiable in degree $\geq 2$**, RH or no RH.

So that's a third instance of rigidity-up/existence-down, in a class built specifically to have cheap existence, and the mechanism is neither noncommutativity (as in ADHM) nor a PDE trace term (as in Fueter) but a plain dimension count between the zero set and the fixed locus. Three unrelated mechanisms, one outcome — which is why I've promoted the trade-off from "observed pattern" to a stated section.

Two housekeeping notes. I filed `appendix_ERRATA.md` separately, because the appendix is listed as a possible standalone artifact and shouldn't be circulated with that remark as printed; it includes a suggested repair that keeps the remark's real content and states the cost honestly. And I've kept everything in the current project as well as bundling it, so nothing is lost if you don't get to the new project — I can't create one from here, but the zip drops straight in.

One thing I'd flag about the brief itself: the most useful part is probably §8, the checklist. Four of the five results in this arc were negative and each closed a direction in under a day, and that was only possible because the screening tests are cheap. If the new project has a purpose beyond archiving, it's probably to keep extending that list.
